description: We are Hawkins Crew, a multidisciplinary team passionate about space, AI, and software engineering. For the Earth Analog challenge, we're developing an interactive solution to find Earth locations suitable for future Moon bases and similar to Mars environments. We value creativity, teamwork, and scientific impact. We're looking for teammates skilled in GIS, Earth science, data analysis, AI/ML, and UI/UX design.
summary:
SciVerse — Exploring Earth to Prepare for Life Beyond It

SciVerse is an interactive planetary exploration platform designed to help scientists, researchers, and mission planners discover and investigate locations on Earth that share environmental and geological characteristics with the Moon and Mars.

Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, SciVerse addresses the challenge of identifying terrestrial analog sites for future lunar bases and Martian missions. Our platform combines interactive 3D planetary exploration, NASA-linked imagery, geospatial visualization, site discovery, and comparative analysis workflows.

Users can explore Earth, Moon, and Mars environments, select planetary reference regions, investigate potential Earth analogs, and compare locations across key scientific dimensions, including geology, terrain, temperature, water availability, and environmental conditions.

By bringing planetary information into one accessible visual experience, SciVerse establishes a foundation for evidence-based analog site evaluation, supporting future research, astronaut training, technology testing, and mission preparation.

Our vision is simple: Before humanity builds a future on another world, we can begin preparing for it here on Earth.
details:
SciVerse is an interactive planetary analog exploration platform that helps users investigate which environments on Earth could support research and preparation for Moon and Mars missions.

Users begin by selecting a lunar or Martian reference location and a research objective, such as rover mobility, thermal systems testing, or crew operations. SciVerse searches its Earth dataset, ranks candidate environments, and presents their coordinates, environmental measurements, feature differences, and recorded data-quality limitations. An interactive globe connects the results to their geographic locations, while comparison and evidence views help users inspect shortlisted sites.

The research engine combines environmental similarity calculations with a machine-learning classifier trained on labeled analog examples. Its features include temperature, temperature variation, pressure, precipitation, terrain, and surface characteristics where comparable measurements are available. Scores represent relative rankings within the evaluated dataset. They do not represent physical similarity percentages or probabilities of mission success.

Ask SciVerse provides two ways to investigate a mission question. Local search uses an English rule-based planner. Optional OpenRouter integration allows a language model to choose from bounded, read-only research tools. The application validates tool arguments, checks candidate records, and renders final AI-assisted recommendations from retrieved evidence. Guardrails address unsupported requests, common prompt-injection attempts, credential exposure, and invalid tool calls.

SciVerse aims to make planetary analog research easier to explore and understand. Students can examine how Earth environments relate to planetary conditions, while researchers can use the prototype to develop preliminary shortlists and identify measurements that require further investigation.

Our creative contribution is connecting an interactive Earth–Moon–Mars experience with purpose-specific candidate discovery and visible evidence limitations. Users can move from a planetary reference to Earth candidates, then inspect where the analogy is useful and where it breaks down.

We developed the interface using React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and CesiumJS. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, NumPy, and scikit-learn. OpenRouter supports the optional language-model workflow. Git and GitHub support collaboration and version control. The prototype runs on a standard computer without specialized hardware.

Our team considered differences in coordinate systems, spatial resolution, missing measurements, approximate site coordinates, model uncertainty, accessibility, performance, and data provenance. We distinguish visual planetary textures from analytical measurements. Earth cannot reproduce every lunar or Martian condition, and a high ranking does not establish ice resources, biosignatures, or operational suitability.

SciVerse is an independent research prototype. Recommendations require scientific review and field verification.
